name: Generate income in place
summary: A unit stops wherever it likes, sets up and earns money for its team for as long as it stays put, with no field to work, nothing to carry and no drop-off. In Command & Conquer: Generals the Hacker sits down with a laptop and draws a small payment every couple of seconds; each payment gives him experience, so he climbs the ranks without fighting, and a top-rank Hacker brings in twice what a new one does. Packing up to move takes a few seconds, and while working he is unarmed and in the open, so the enemy's answer is to find the earner and kill it; some versions earn faster, and more safely, inside a friendly building. Unlike gather-resources, there is no node, route or bank to raid: only the earner itself.
counterplay: Hunt the earner: it has no weapon and sits still, so any soldier, vehicle or aircraft that finds it gets an easy kill and stops the income at once; the Generals wiki notes that vehicles simply run Hackers over.
Strike early: a new earner brings in little and grows with every rank, so a kill before it ranks up costs the enemy the most future income.
Force it to move: packing up takes a few seconds, so even a threat makes it stop earning and leaves it slow to escape.

Search the quiet corners: it can set up anywhere, so scouts must sweep the places nobody watches, and a camouflaged earner such as the Infantry General's Hacker stays hidden even while it earns, so bring detection (the Generals wiki names Pathfinder snipers).
Hit the shelter: earners working inside a friendly building, such as Hackers in an Internet Center, are safe only while it stands, so the building becomes the target.
Use toxins or radiation where they exist: the Hacker has no protection against them.

other_examples.unit: Command units and the Resource Allocation System
other_examples.note: Every command unit produces a trickle of mass and energy by itself, wherever it stands, with no deposit or extractor. The Resource Allocation System upgrade, open to the main commander and to the support commanders summoned from a Quantum Gateway, raises that output a great deal (the Aeon and Seraphim commanders can take it in two steps), so a sturdy builder becomes a walking power plant that keeps earning while it moves and fights. Installing an upgrade roots the commander in place for a while, though it can still shoot back, and losing the main commander loses an Assassination game.

sources.title: UEF T3 Support Armored Command Unit, Supreme Commander Wiki
sources.note: Its upgrade list includes the Resource Allocation System, which raises the support commander's production.

other_examples.note: Greek players earn favor, the resource behind myth units, myth technologies and reused god powers, by sending villagers to a temple, where they stand and pray instead of gathering. Each extra worshipper adds less than the one before, so a handful at a time is usually enough, and every praying villager is one not working food, wood or gold. The wiki calls the method flexible and safe, since praying uses up nothing but the villagers' time.

sources.title: Greeks (Age of Mythology), Age of Empires Series Wiki
Favor, Age of Empires Series Wiki

other_examples.note: A building card that pumps out one elixir at a steady pace for as long as it lasts, and one more when it is destroyed. It is expensive to place, which leaves its owner open to a rush for a while, and over its whole life it pays back only a little more than it cost. The opponent has to answer it: a damaging spell shortens how much it can produce, a Rocket can wipe it out before it pays anything, and a player with no way to reach it is advised to attack hard instead, so the owner has no time to build strong pushes with the extra.

shooter_analogues.note: Besides healing and refilling teammates nearby, a built Dispenser slowly refills a store of metal, the Engineer's building currency, which friendly Engineers draw from, and each upgrade raises its output. It has no weapon and takes a long time to build up to full strength, so the wiki advises tucking it around a corner where enemies can't shoot it and in sight of the team's Sentry Gun, and it stresses that destroying it slows the defenders' recovery. A destroyed Dispenser leaves scrap metal that players of either team can pick up.

player_translation.summary: A cheap, unarmed T2 support card. On a key it sets up wherever its player likes and then earns team money every few seconds for as long as it stays put, ranking up as it earns so that each rank pays more. It can't fight while set up and needs a moment to pack up, so its game is choosing hidden, safe spots and leaving before hunters arrive; the enemy's game is finding it.
as_user: You buy a cheap card with no real weapon. Press the key to unpack: after a short set-up you earn a payment for the team every few seconds, and a bar shows how close you are to the next rank.
Every payment gives you experience, so you rank up without fighting and each rank raises your pay; staying alive is the whole job.

You pick spots the enemy won't check: behind your lines, in a dead-end corner, inside a friendly shelter. Packing up takes a few seconds, so you leave when hunters are on their way, not when they arrive.
Your team's money grows faster while you live, so you call for an escort when a hunter finds you.
as_target: Somewhere on the map an enemy earner is feeding their team's money. A faint signal pulse every so often gives its rough direction, so hunting it is worth a detour.
Once found it can't shoot back and is slow to pack up: rush it, snipe it or drop splash on it. A high-rank earner, shown by its badge, is the bigger prize.
Killing it stops its income at once and resets its rank, so the enemy's next earner starts from the bottom.
teammates: The earner's team: an escort or a friendly turret near its spot keeps it alive, and the money it brings lets everyone buy better cards sooner.
The enemy team: scouts and raiders hunt the earner, and a scout who spots it should ping it so a hunter can finish it.
Each extra earner on a team pays less than the one before, as each extra worshipper does in Age of Mythology, so one or two earners are enough and the rest of the team fights.
controls: Q: set up or pack up, a deploy on one counted key; both take a moment, shown by a progress ring.
The card's main fire is at most a weak sidearm, or nothing at all.
Middle mouse, the universal ping: 'earner here, guard me'.
feedback: A laptop or antenna unfolds over the model, and a soft coin tick plays with each payment; teammates see small money pop-ups.
A rank badge and a progress bar to the next rank, visible to both teams, so a high-rank earner reads as a prize.
A periodic signal pulse that enemies see as a direction cue on their screen edge, so the earner can be hunted rather than only stumbled upon.
changes_from_rts: A Generals player can tuck Hackers away at the back of the base for the whole game. Players need a reason and a way to hunt the earner, so it gives off a faint, periodic signal while working.
Generals puts no cap on Hackers, and every player could buy an earner; each extra earner on a team should pay less, and the total should be capped.
A Generals Hacker keeps his ranks until he dies; keep that, so a long-lived earner becomes a prize, and reset on death so a kill matters.
Generals' Internet Center houses up to eight Hackers in safety; a shelter for earners is a higher-spice variant, because it makes them hard to kill.
Money in a team shooter has to reach teammates visibly and credit the earner, or nobody will pick a card that never fights.

team_play.notes: Valuable to the whole team but helpless alone: the earner needs an escort or a hidden spot, the enemy needs scouts and raiders to find it, and a guarded earner makes good bait for an ambush.

notes: A deployed state with set-up and pack-up timers, shared with deploy-siege-mode, plus a payment timer that feeds team money.
Experience per payment and rank thresholds can reuse the veterancy system.
A signal or reveal rule so enemies can find the earner, and lower pay for each extra earner on a team.
Payments decided by the server, paused while packing or disabled.
Income compounds: money buys better cards, which protect the earner, which earns more. Cap the total and pay each extra earner less.
An earner hidden where nobody looks could decide a match without a fight; the signal rule and the cap prevent that.
If the pay is too small to matter, nobody picks the card; tune it against the value of a kill on the earner.
The enemy can't see income directly; the signal pulse or the scoreboard must show that an earner is working.
Set-up, earning and pack-up need distinct animations, so hunters know when the earner can't escape.

variants.name: Set up and earn
variants.summary: Deploy anywhere and earn a payment every few seconds while set up, ranking up with the payments; pack up to move. The basic version.

variants.name: Pray at a shrine
variants.summary: Earn only while standing at a friendly shrine or point, with each extra worker there earning less; the spot is safe, but every worker standing at it is out of the fight.
variants.seen_in: Age of Mythology Greek temple worship

variants.name: Sheltered earners
variants.summary: Earners can work from inside a friendly shelter that holds several of them and pays a little faster; they are safe while it stands, so the shelter becomes the enemy's target.
variants.seen_in: Generals Internet Center (holds up to eight Hackers)

variants.name: Camouflaged earner
variants.summary: Hidden even while it earns. It shows itself only while it uses its other hacks or when a detector finds it, and once found, idle enemies that can see it go for it, so hunters need stealth detection.

countered_by.why: It stays hidden even while it earns, so only a detector can find it; the Generals wiki names Pathfinder snipers, which spot the Infantry General's Hacker and kill it from far away.
Once revealed it has nothing that shoots upward, and the Generals wiki counts aircraft among the attackers that strike the Infantry General's Hacker from beyond its reach.
Once revealed it is still unarmed and slow to pack up, so vehicles run it down; the Generals wiki notes that vehicles simply run Hackers over.

variants.name: Placed collector
variants.summary: Instead of sitting down, place a collector that pumps out money for a limited lifetime and pays a little more when destroyed; it costs a lot up front, and the enemy can spend a strike or a raid to kill it before it pays off.
variants.seen_in: Clash Royale Elixir Collector; Team Fortress 2 Dispenser's metal store

variants.name: Walking generator
variants.summary: A costly upgrade makes a sturdy unit produce money by itself all the time, even while moving and fighting, so there is no set-up to catch it in, only a big price up front.
variants.seen_in: Supreme Commander command units with the Resource Allocation System

adds_strengths.why: Earns money for the whole team wherever it sets up, with no field or route to defend, and earns more with every rank it gains.

adds_weaknesses.why: Unarmed and rooted while it earns, and slow to pack up, so anything that finds it can kill it and stop the income.

countered_by.why: Vehicles run an unarmed earner down before it can pack up; the Generals wiki notes that vehicles simply run Hackers over.
An unarmed earner has nothing that shoots upward, and the Generals wiki counts aircraft among the attackers that pick off Hackers from beyond their reach.
It hides by setting up where nobody looks, so scouts who find and mark it hand their team an easy kill.

open_questions: How should the enemy find a hidden earner: a periodic signal, a reveal after some time in one spot, or scouting alone?
Should the income go to the whole team equally, or partly to the earner for its own upgrades?
Should ranks earned by earning reset on death?
How many earners may a team run before each extra one pays less, and should the total be capped?

shooter_fit.reason: A clear role for players who like supporting, and the hide-and-hunt loop suits a team shooter, but a card that never fights is hard to make fun and unchecked income snowballs, so it needs a signal for hunters and falling pay for extra earners.
